name: Identifiable victim effect
statement: People are said to give more to one named and pictured victim than to statistics about many, but the pooled effect is small and preregistered replications have not found it.
meaning: The claim compares two ways of describing the same need. One names a person, gives an age, and shows a photograph. The other gives a number. Helping is held to be higher in the first case, which would mean charity tracks how a cause is presented rather than how much good the money does. Three mechanisms are usually offered. Proportion dominance says an identified victim is her own reference group, so helping her rescues 100% of those at risk. The affect heuristic says a specific face produces sympathy and a number does not. Perceived impact says people give when they can picture what the money changes. The three make different predictions, and the literature has not settled which of them, if any, is carrying the effect.

origin.who: Karen E. Jenni and George Loewenstein
origin.note: Their paper is titled "Explaining the 'Identifiable Victim Effect'" and opens by quoting Thomas Schelling's 1968 discussion of the individual and the statistical life, which Lee and Feeley credit as the first treatment. Jenni and Loewenstein took the effect as given and tested four candidate causes; the effect itself was not what they set out to demonstrate.

evidence: Jenni and Loewenstein ran two hypothetical scenario studies, on 127 respondents drawn from Carnegie Mellon, a Boston shopping mall and two student centres, and on 121 visitors to Pittsburgh airport. Nothing was donated. Respondents rated how important an intervention was, or how responsible they would feel. Only one of the four candidate causes came through cleanly. People cared more about saving 25 of 25 casualties than 25 of 50,000, which is proportion of the reference group. Vividness did nothing. In the second study, where a trapped earthquake victim was described generically, described in detail, or described with a photograph, respondents said they cared least when the photograph was included, and the differences did not reach significance. Small, Loewenstein and Slovic put real money on the table ten years later. Participants at a university in Pennsylvania completed an unrelated survey, were paid five one-dollar bills, and could seal any of it into an envelope for Save the Children. The money went to the charity. Study 1, on 121 people, found an identifiable victim raised donations to $2.12 against $1.21 for statistics, F(1, 115) = 6.75, p < .05, partial eta squared .06. Study 3, on 159 people, produced the pair everyone quotes: $2.38 for Rokia, a seven-year-old girl from Mali shown with a photograph, against $1.14 for four sentences of famine statistics about Malawi, Zambia, Angola and Ethiopia. Presenting Rokia together with the statistics dropped giving to $1.43, and the paper's argument is about that drop rather than about the gap. Kogut and Ritov added the singularity claim, that the effect holds for one victim and not for a group. Majumder and colleagues describe their 2005 Study 2 as 120 Hebrew University undergraduates in a two-by-two design, with a singularity by identifiability interaction at p = .009, partial eta squared .062. The name singularity effect comes from the title of Kogut and Ritov's second 2005 paper, in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes. Majumder's group define it as the tendency to give more aid to one victim than to a group facing the same need.

replication.headline: Two preregistered replications of the two seminal papers found nothing, and a bias-corrected reanalysis of the meta-analysis puts the pooled effect at r = 0.002.
replication.detail: Lee and Feeley pooled 41 effects and reported r = .05, z = 2.07, p < .05, 95% CI .003 to .10, with heterogeneity Q(40) = 104.65, p < .001 and I2 = 61.8%. Their own summary sentence is "the IVE effect is small". They inspected a funnel plot and saw no serious asymmetry. Maier, Wong and Feldman reanalysed the same 41 effects with robust Bayesian meta-analysis and reached the opposite reading: moderate evidence for publication bias, BF01 = 0.11, strong evidence for the absence of an average effect, BF01 = 14.93, and a model-averaged estimate of r = 0.002, 95% CI 0 to 0.004. They note that the largest study in the dataset, with 12,802 participants, returns r = 0.004. Their own preregistered replication of Small, Loewenstein and Slovic's Studies 1 and 3, on 1,004 MTurk participants, found no identifiable victim effect, partial eta squared .000, 95% CI .000 to .003, and no debiasing effect, .001, 95% CI .000 to .012. Identifiable against statistical came out at t(998) = 0.097, p = 1.00, d = 0.01, 95% CI -0.16 to 0.14, with a Bayes factor of 11.57 favouring the null. Majumder, Tai, Ziano and Feldman preregistered a close replication of Kogut and Ritov's Study 2 on 1,835 participants after exclusions, and found the singularity by identifiability interaction at partial eta squared .00, 90% CI 0.00 to 0.00. Outside the laboratory, Lesner and Rasmussen mailed 25,797 prior donors of a Danish charity either an identifiable or a statistical appeal and report that the identifiable letter "did not result in significantly larger donations". Moche, Karlsson and Västfjäll ran five studies on 7,996 people and found no identifiability effect in three of them; in a fourth the unidentified condition gave more, F(1, 1624) = 16.27, p < .001, partial eta squared .010.

study.cite: Maier, M., Wong, Y. C., & Feldman, G. (2024). Revisiting and rethinking the identifiable victim effect: Replication and extension of Small, Loewenstein, and Slovic (2007). Collabra: Psychology, 9(1), 90203.

limits: No well-powered replication has used real money. Both preregistered failures asked for hypothetical donations, and Maier and colleagues say so themselves, calling for high-powered replications with real money run as registered reports and in collaboration with proponents of the effect. That gap matters, because Lee and Feeley's own moderator analysis found the mean effect reached significance only in the subgroup where actual monetary contributions were measured, r = .08, and in the field-study subgroup, r = .13. How many of their 41 effects came from real money rather than stated intentions could not be established: their Table 2 is behind a paywall and could not be retrieved, and the counts are not given in the text. The heterogeneity is real, so a single pooled number describes the literature poorly. The effect also does not travel across recipients. Deshpande and Spears ran three randomised experiments in India and report an identifiable victim effect for generic and high-caste recipients that is "absent or even reversed for low-caste recipients". This entry found no multi-laboratory replication project covering the effect. Bhati and Hansen, reviewing 187 experimental fundraising papers published between 2007 and 2019, add a separate objection: studies of the identified victim often stereotype the beneficiary in order to produce guilt in the donor.
misreadings: The famous pair of numbers is one study, not the paper. The $2.38 against $1.14 comes from Study 3 of Small, Loewenstein and Slovic, and that paper's other three studies are less obliging. Study 2, on 99 people, found no main effect of identifiability at all, F(1, 95) = .073, p = .79. Study 4, on 165 people, likewise found none, F(1, 160) = .87, p = .35. The paper is a study of what deliberation does to giving, not a demonstration that faces beat numbers. Its Study 4 also reports the same two F statistics for both the main effects and the simple effects, with different p values attached, which the entry could not reconcile. The second misreading is about what the effect is a contrast with. Lee and Feeley found the pooled effect largest when the unidentified comparison was a single victim, r = .13, and near zero when it was a group, r = .01. It also reversed when the identified side was a group rather than one person, r = -.09, 95% CI -.19 to .001, across eight effects. So the reliable pattern is one identified person against one unidentified person, which is not the mass-versus-individual story the effect is usually told as. Third, the photograph. Fundraising advice treats a face as the active ingredient, and Lee and Feeley do find the effect only in studies that used one. Jenni and Loewenstein found the opposite in the paper that named the effect, with the photographed victim drawing the least concern. Finally, the Baby Jessica anecdote. Jenni and Loewenstein date the rescue to late 1987 and Lee and Feeley to 1987; the stimulus text Small, Loewenstein and Slovic gave their participants says 1989, while their own introduction says 1987.
